He's been living at his cabin for five weeks and hasn't traveled recently. He doesn't smoke or use illicit drugs.

His vital signs are: temp 99°F (which is slightly elevated, maybe a low-grade fever), BP 130/78 (which is okay, a bit on the lower side but not too bad), pulse 72/min (normal), and oxygen at 98% on room air. He's asymptomatic in the office, and the physical exam didn't show anything unusual.

The labs are notable for a hemoglobin of 20 g/dL and hematocrit of 60%. Those are both elevated. Normal hemoglobin for men is around 13.5-17.5 g/dL, so 20 is definitely high. Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells, so 60% is also elevated. His leukocyte count is normal, and platelets are fine too.

So, putting this together. The headaches and dizziness are concerning. The fact that they get better when he's outside makes me think about environmental factors. Dehydration can cause headaches and dizziness, but why would going outside help? Maybe the cabin has poor air quality or something else. 

Looking at his medications, I know that amlodipine can sometimes cause headaches as a side effect. But that's usually mild and doesn't explain the dizziness and nausea. His diabetes medications are metformin and glimepiride. Metformin can cause gastrointestinal issues, but he's had this for a month, and the symptoms are more about headaches and dizziness. 

The elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit suggest polycythemia. Polycythemia can be primary (a disease where the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells) or secondary (due to some other condition). Secondary causes include chronic hypoxia, dehydration, or certain cancers. 

He's been living in a cabin for five weeks. Maybe the cabin has poor ventilation, leading to low oxygen levels inside. But he's been at the cabin, maybe not drinking enough, but his symptoms are more about headaches and dizziness, which can also be dehydration-related. However, the fact that stepping outside helps points more towards environmental factors like low oxygen.

He doesn't smoke, so that's not contributing to carbon monoxide issues. His medical history doesn't include anything that would directly cause polycythemia except maybe his asthma, but that's usually not a cause unless it's severe. 

Looking at his medications, none of them typically cause polycythemia. So, the most likely diagnosis is secondary polycythemia, probably due to chronic hypoxia from living in a poorly ventilated cabin. The labs show a high hemoglobin of 20 g/dL and hematocrit of 60%, which are both above normal. His leukocytes are normal, and platelets are also within normal range. 

Hmm. High Hgb and Hct usually point to dehydration, but he's been at home, not traveling, and his symptoms aren't typical of dehydration. Dehydration usually causes more acute symptoms, and he's had this for a month. Plus, he's asymptomatic in the office, which doesn't fit with severe dehydration. 

Another possibility is living at a high altitude. His cabin is upstate, maybe at higher elevation. High altitude can cause headaches, dizziness, and nausea because of lower oxygen levels. His symptoms get better when he's outside, which might be because he's getting more oxygen when he's moving around, even if it's just shoveling. 

His body might be responding to the altitude by increasing red blood cell production to carry more oxygen, which would explain the elevated Hgb and Hct. This is called polycythemia, which can be a response to chronic hypoxia. 

He doesn't have any symptoms of an infection since his WBC is normal, and his other vitals don't suggest that. No smoking or drug use, so no other causes of high Hgb. 

Putting it all together, his symptoms and lab results align with altitude sickness. The high Hgb is likely a physiologic response to the lower oxygen at higher altitude. His body is making more red blood cells to compensate, which is why the Hct is up. The headaches and dizziness are classic signs of altitude-related issues.
